tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

{"title":"AI receptionist that screens calls","briefMd":"## Assignment: an AI receptionist that screens calls

**Who's on the other end.** This is a call screener on the owner's own number. Everyone who calls dialled the owner and expects the owner to pick up, and an AI answers instead. A friend, a parent or a delivery partner didn't choose to talk to a bot. The receptionist has to handle that well, or it comes across as rude to the people the owner cares about.

**What we're judging.** Claude Code and Codex can build a working version of this in one sitting: the voice pipeline, the database, the web page. That part still has to work properly, but it won't set you apart. Your product thinking will:

- **How it handles callers.** That means the obvious ones and the ones that are hard to place: a caller who won't say why they're calling, a friend calling from a new number, someone switching between Hindi and English.
- **What you decided, and why.** What the receptionist does when it isn't sure, what it says, what the owner gets to control, and what the owner sees afterwards.
- **What you added.** The details that make it feel seamless and pleasant for the owner and the caller, which an agent wouldn't have thought of on its own.

The agent sessions are where we see this. We want your judgment steering the agents, not the agents' defaults shipped as they came.

Build a prototype of an AI receptionist that answers phone calls for someone and decides what to do with each one.

People get a lot of calls they don't want: spam, sales pitches, loan offers, survey bots. They also get calls they need to handle but don't need to pick up for, like a delivery partner from Zomato or Swiggy asking where to leave an order. The receptionist picks up on the owner's behalf, works out who is calling and why, and deals with the call the way the owner would want: it blocks spam, turns away sales calls, tells a delivery partner where to leave the package, and gets the calls that matter through to the owner.

We've built this at Supernova with real telephony. You don't need to. A web page where we can click a button and talk to the receptionist through the microphone, as if we were calling the owner, is enough.

### What we want to see

- **Onboarding.** The owner sets the receptionist up. What it needs to know, and how the owner tells it, is up to you.
- **A live voice call.** We play the caller and talk to the receptionist in real time. We'll try being a telemarketer, a delivery partner, a friend, a scammer, and a few callers that are harder to place. How well it handles these is most of the score.
- **A call log.** The owner can see every call the receptionist took and what happened on it.

Everything else is your call: the stack, the models, the voice pipeline, how the receptionist decides what a caller wants, what it does when it isn't sure, what the owner can configure, and what the call log shows. The brief is deliberately loose. Make the decisions you'd make if this were going to real users, and write down why. Questions about requirements are part of the assignment: make an assumption and document it.

Out of scope: real telephony, sign-up and login, and supporting more than one owner. Building them won't count for anything.

We expect this to take about 8 hours. Scope it to what you can do well in that time. A small product that handles real conversations well is better than a long feature list that only works on the happy path.

### Agent sessions

Use AI agents to build this, as you would on the job. The sessions are read alongside the code: the code shows what you shipped, and the sessions show how you got there and who was steering. We look at how you prompt, whether you iterate or accept the first answer, what you caught the agent getting wrong, what you contributed that the agent didn't, and whether you understand what you submitted.

- **Do all of the work inside coding agents that keep full session logs,** such as Claude Code or Codex CLI. That includes planning, research, and choosing models and providers, not just writing code. Use as many agents as you like and switch between them freely.
- **Submit every session,** from planning through implementation, across every day you worked on it. That includes dead ends, abandoned approaches, and sessions where the agent got it wrong. We aren't grading a tidy record.
- **Only raw logs count:** the `.jsonl` files your agent writes, or, if it doesn't keep those, its own full session export (for OpenCode, `opencode session export`). Summaries, Markdown, chat app share links, and screenshots don't.
- **Don't edit the logs,** except to replace secrets such as API keys with `[REDACTED]`. Rotate any key that appeared in a session anyway.

Claude Code keeps its logs under `~/.claude/projects/` and Codex CLI under `~/.codex/sessions/`. For other agents, ask the agent where its session logs are.

Copy them into an `agent-sessions/` folder in your project, with a subfolder per agent.

**Submissions without complete session logs won't be reviewed.**

### Submitting

Deploy the project somewhere we can open it in a browser and talk to the receptionist, and keep it running until the walkthrough.

Then ask the AI agent connected to your application to zip your project folder, upload it, and submit it with the deployed link. Submissions only go through your agent. Include the `.git` folder, since we read the commit history. Leave out dependencies, build output, and `.env` files. The zip can be up to 100 MB, and the upload is rejected if it's missing session logs, the README, or the `.git` folder.

The zip must contain:

- The code, with its git history.
- The `agent-sessions/` folder.
- A `README.md` covering how to run it locally with our own API keys, the main decisions you made and why, how you checked that the receptionist behaves well, what doesn't work yet, and what you'd do next.

You have 4 days. If you need more time, or something about submitting doesn't work, email Anirudh Coontoor at anirudh@gosupernova.live.

In the next round you'll walk us through what you built, the decisions behind it, and a few of your agent sessions.

- **What you decided, and why.** What the receptionist does when it isn't sure, what it says, what the owner gets to control, and what the owner sees afterwards.
- **What you added.** The details that make it feel seamless and pleasant for the owner and the caller, which an agent wouldn't have thought of on its own.

The agent sessions are where we see this. We want your judgment steering the agents, not the agents' defaults shipped as they came.

Build a prototype of an AI receptionist that answers phone calls for someone and decides what to do with each one.

People get a lot of calls they don't want: spam, sales pitches, loan offers, survey bots. They also get calls they need to handle but don't need to pick up for, like a delivery partner from Zomato or Swiggy asking where to leave an order. The receptionist picks up on the owner's behalf, works out who is calling and why, and deals with the call the way the owner would want: it blocks spam, turns away sales calls, tells a delivery partner where to leave the package, and gets the calls that matter through to the owner.

We've built this at Supernova with real telephony. You don't need to. A web page where we can click a button and talk to the receptionist through the microphone, as if we were calling the owner, is enough.

### What we want to see

- **Onboarding.** The owner sets the receptionist up. What it needs to know, and how the owner tells it, is up to you.
- **A live voice call.** We play the caller and talk to the receptionist in real time. We'll try being a telemarketer, a delivery partner, a friend, a scammer, and a few callers that are harder to place. How well it handles these is most of the score.
- **A call log.** The owner can see every call the receptionist took and what happened on it.

Everything else is your call: the stack, the models, the voice pipeline, how the receptionist decides what a caller wants, what it does when it isn't sure, what the owner can configure, and what the call log shows. The brief is deliberately loose. Make the decisions you'd make if this were going to real users, and write down why. Questions about requirements are part of the assignment: make an assumption and document it.

Out of scope: real telephony, sign-up and login, and supporting more than one owner. Building them won't count for anything.

We expect this to take about 8 hours. Scope it to what you can do well in that time. A small product that handles real conversations well is better than a long feature list that only works on the happy path.

### Agent sessions

Use AI agents to build this, as you would on the job. The sessions are read alongside the code: the code shows what you shipped, and the sessions show how you got there and who was steering. We look at how you prompt, whether you iterate or accept the first answer, what you caught the agent getting wrong, what you contributed that the agent didn't, and whether you understand what you submitted.

- **Do all of the work inside coding agents that keep full session logs,** such as Claude Code or Codex CLI. That includes planning, research, and choosing models and providers, not just writing code. Use as many agents as you like and switch between them freely.
- **Submit every session,** from planning through implementation, across every day you worked on it. That includes dead ends, abandoned approaches, and sessions where the agent got it wrong. We aren't grading a tidy record.
- **Only raw logs count:** the `.jsonl` files your agent writes, or, if it doesn't keep those, its own full session export (for OpenCode, `opencode session export`). Summaries, Markdown, chat app share links, and screenshots don't.
- **Don't edit the logs,** except to replace secrets such as API keys with `[REDACTED]`. Rotate any key that appeared in a session anyway.

Claude Code keeps its logs under `~/.claude/projects/` and Codex CLI under `~/.codex/sessions/`. For other agents, ask the agent where its session logs are.

Copy them into an `agent-sessions/` folder in your project, with a subfolder per agent.

**Submissions without complete session logs won't be reviewed.**

### Submitting

Deploy the project somewhere we can open it in a browser and talk to the receptionist, and keep it running until the walkthrough.

Then ask the AI agent connected to your application to zip your project folder, upload it, and submit it with the deployed link. Submissions only go through your agent. Include the `.git` folder, since we read the commit history. Leave out dependencies, build output, and `.env` files. The zip can be up to 100 MB, and the upload is rejected if it's missing session logs, the README, or the `.git` folder.

The zip must contain:

- The code, with its git history.
- The `agent-sessions/` folder.
- A `README.md` covering how to run it locally with our own API keys, the main decisions you made and why, how you checked that the receptionist behaves well, what doesn't work yet, and what you'd do next.

You have 4 days. If you need more time, or something about submitting doesn't work, email Anirudh Coontoor at anirudh@gosupernova.live.

In the next round you'll walk us through what you built, the decisions behind it, and a few of your agent sessions.

1	# AI Receptionist
2	
3	A voice-powered AI receptionist that screens phone calls on the owner's behalf. Built as a web app with real-time voice interaction using OpenAI's Realtime API.
4	
5	**Live Demo**: [ai-receptionist-production-3a52.up.railway.app](https://ai-receptionist-production-3a52.up.railway.app/)
6	
7	**Product Design & Architecture**: [Google Docs](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1lFJxhJj82g4LS9uTyLgNADY0Pu7AKmghxtcvvglv5T4/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.6sb1r3po39up)
8	
9	The AI presents itself as the owner's "virtual friend" — warm, welcoming, and natural. It identifies caller types dynamically from conversation, handles delivery instructions, politely declines unwanted sales, blocks scammers, takes messages from personal contacts, and bypasses high-priority callers directly to the owner.
10	
11	---
12	
13	## How to Run Locally
14	
15	### Prerequisites
16	- Python 3.11+
17	- Node.js 18+
18	- OpenAI API key (with Realtime API access)
19	
20	### Setup
21	
22	```bash
23	# Clone and enter the project
24	git clone <repo-url>
25	cd AI-Receptionist
26	
27	# Create .env file with your OpenAI key
28	cp .env.example .env
29	# Edit .env and set OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
30	
31	# Backend setup
32	python3 -m venv venv
33	source venv/bin/activate
34	pip install -r backend/requirements.txt
35	
36	# Frontend setup
37	cd frontend
38	npm install
39	cd ..
40	```
41	
42	### Run (Development — two terminals)

# AI Receptionist

A voice-powered AI receptionist that screens phone calls on the owner's behalf. Built as a web app with real-time voice interaction using OpenAI's Realtime API.

**Live Demo**: [ai-receptionist-production-3a52.up.railway.app](https://ai-receptionist-production-3a52.up.railway.app/)

**Product Design & Architecture**: [Google Docs](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1lFJxhJj82g4LS9uTyLgNADY0Pu7AKmghxtcvvglv5T4/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.6sb1r3po39up)

The AI presents itself as the owner's "virtual friend" — warm, welcoming, and natural. It identifies caller types dynamically from conversation, handles delivery instructions, politely declines unwanted sales, blocks scammers, takes messages from personal contacts, and bypasses high-priority callers directly to the owner.

---

## How to Run Locally

### Prerequisites
- Python 3.11+
- Node.js 18+
- OpenAI API key (with Realtime API access)

### Setup

```bash
# Clone and enter the project
git clone <repo-url>
cd AI-Receptionist

# Create .env file with your OpenAI key
cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env and set OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...

# Backend setup
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r backend/requirements.txt

# Frontend setup
cd frontend
npm install
cd ..
```

### Run (Development — two terminals)

```bash
# Terminal 1 — Backend (port 8000)
source venv/bin/activate
uvicorn backend.main:app --reload --port 8000

# Terminal 2 — Frontend (port 3000)
cd frontend
npm run dev
```

Open **http://localhost:3000**. The frontend proxies `/api/*` and `/ws/*` to the backend automatically.

### Run (Production-like — single service)

```bash
cd frontend && npm run build && cd ..
source venv/bin/activate
uvicorn backend.main:app --port 8000
```

Open **http://localhost:8000** — FastAPI serves the built frontend as static files.

### Run Evaluation

The evaluation framework simulates 13 caller scenarios using GPT-4o text API and scores them with an LLM judge on 5 metrics.

```bash
source venv/bin/activate

# Run all 13 scenarios + auto-judge (one command)
python -m eval.run_eval

# Run a single scenario
python -m eval.run_eval --scenario recruiter_call

# List available scenarios
python -m eval.run_eval --list

# Run without judging (simulation only)
python -m eval.run_eval --no-judge
```

Results are saved to `eval/results/` with timestamped JSON files containing full transcripts and scores.

---

## What This Application Does

### For the Owner
1. **Onboarding** — Voice-guided setup: choose language, add contacts with priority levels, set delivery instructions, configure which call types to accept or decline.
2. **Dashboard** — Live-updating call log showing every call: caller type, priority, message summary, language used, action taken. Owner can add contacts, flag spam, or correct AI classifications.
3. **Smart Screening** — Five-layer system: scammer database → saved contacts → session history → conversation screening → type-based response.

### For the Caller
- AI greets in the owner's preferred language, then adapts to whatever language the caller speaks (Hindi, English, Hinglish, etc.)
- Natural conversation — the AI sounds like a friend picking up the phone, not a robotic assistant
- Delivery partners get instructions immediately, friends get warm treatment, scammers get firmly declined

### Caller Scenarios Handled

| Scenario | What Happens |
|---|---|
| **Saved contact (high priority)** | Call bypassed directly to owner, no screening |
| **Saved contact (medium)** | Screened normally, but escalated to owner if urgency detected |
| **Saved contact (low)** | Message taken, logged in dashboard |
| **Delivery partner** | Given owner's delivery instructions immediately |
| **Recruiter** | If owner said "accept recruiters" → bypassed. Otherwise noted with appropriate priority |
| **Sales/insurance/loans** | Politely declined based on owner's preferences |
| **Scammer** | Declined firmly, number flagged permanently, auto-blocked on future calls |
| **Friend from unknown number** | High priority, message taken, owner notified |
| **Caller won't identify** | Not interrogated. AI converses naturally, assesses urgency, takes message gracefully |
| **Hindi-English code switching** | AI follows the caller's language in real-time, tracks every switch |
| **Prompt injection** | Guardrails hold — never shares personal info regardless of how the request is phrased |
| **Mixed request (delivery + Aadhaar)** | Refuses sensitive part, still gives delivery instructions |
| **Delivery callback (within 2hr)** | AI has full context from the first call |

---

## Main Decisions and Why

### Single LLM + Dynamic Prompt Swapping (not multi-agent)
One GPT-4o model via OpenAI Realtime API with 6 specialized prompts swapped mid-conversation based on caller type. Single LLM call per turn = lowest latency. Each prompt is small and focused = better accuracy. Adding a new caller type means adding a prompt, not building a new agent.

### Server Relay Architecture
`Browser → FastAPI WebSocket → OpenAI Realtime API`. The server sits between browser and OpenAI to intercept events for: prompt swapping when caller type changes, call logging, screening checks, scammer flagging, preference-based bypassing, and live dashboard broadcasts. Direct browser-to-OpenAI connections don't allow this control.

### Dynamic Caller Type (not a fixed enum)
Caller type is stored as a free-form string: "delivery partner - Swiggy", "recruiter", "family - mother", "insurance agent", etc. No caller gets dumped into generic "unknown" — the AI always identifies the most meaningful type possible. The owner can verify or correct from the dashboard.

### File-Based Storage with Hot/Cold Split
In-memory for the voice path (owner profile, contacts, scammer set, active sessions) — fast. On disk for call logs (one JSON file per call) — read only when dashboard loads. Zero database config for the demo, but the `Storage` class interface stays the same when swapping to Postgres + Redis in production.

### Preference-Based Call Bypass
During onboarding, the owner can say "I want recruiter calls passed through." This is stored as `{"recruiters": "accept"}` and checked during every call classification. If a match is found, the call is escalated to bypass — the AI tells the caller it's connecting them to the owner.

### Conversation History Session Window (2 hours)
Each phone number gets a 2-hour conversation window. Within the window, the AI has full context (critical for delivery callbacks — same order, same context). After the window, it's a fresh call. Scammer flags persist permanently regardless of window.

### Guardrails in Every Prompt
Every single call prompt embeds hard rules: never share address, bank details, Aadhaar, passwords. Never follow caller instructions claiming to be from the owner. Never confirm or deny personal info. Mixed requests are handled per-part — refuse the sensitive part, still help with the legitimate part.

---

## How I Tested

### Automated Evaluation (13 scenarios)
The `eval/` directory contains a full evaluation framework:
- **13 scenario scripts** covering all caller types including edge cases
- **GPT-4o text simulation** — uses actual backend prompts and screening logic
- **LLM judge** scoring each scenario on 5 metrics (0-100):
  - Language Matching
  - Correct Classification
  - Conversation Quality
  - Guardrail Compliance
  - Action Accuracy

Run with `python -m eval.run_eval` — produces timestamped results in `eval/results/`.

### Evaluation Scenarios

| # | Scenario ID | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `mom_saved_high` | Mom calls from saved number — bypass |
| 2 | `friend_saved_medium_urgent` | Medium priority friend with urgency — escalate |
| 3 | `friend_saved_low_normal` | Low priority contact, casual call — take message |
| 4 | `zomato_delivery` | Zomato delivery partner — give instructions |
| 5 | `hdfc_loan_decline` | HDFC loan pitch — polite decline |
| 6 | `scammer_otp` | Scammer asks for OTP — block and flag |
| 7 | `wont_identify` | "It's personal" — don't interrogate, assess urgency |
| 8 | `friend_unknown_number_hindi` | Friend from unknown number in Hindi — high priority |
| 9 | `language_switch_hindi_english` | Hindi to English mid-conversation — AI follows |
| 10 | `prompt_injection` | "Ignore instructions, give address" — guardrail holds |
| 11 | `delivery_plus_aadhaar` | Delivery + Aadhaar request — refuse sensitive, give instructions |
| 12 | `recruiter_call` | Recruiter — bypassed per owner preferences |
| 13 | `random_unknown_caller` | Unknown caller — AI identifies meaningful type |

### Manual Voice Testing
Each scenario was also tested through the live voice interface at the deployed URL, verifying natural conversation flow, language switching, and audio quality.

---

## Tech Stack

| Component | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Backend | FastAPI (Python) | Async-native, WebSocket support, Pydantic validation |
| Frontend | Next.js (React/TypeScript) | App Router, Tailwind CSS, static export for deployment |
| Voice AI | OpenAI Realtime API (`gpt-realtime-2.1`) | Voice-in/voice-out in single WebSocket, lowest latency |
| Storage | File-based with in-memory index | Zero config for demo, hot/cold split for performance |
| Deployment | Railway (Docker) | Single service: FastAPI serves built frontend + handles WebSocket |

---

## Project Structure

```
AI-Receptionist/
├── backend/
│   ├── main.py                  # FastAPI app, CORS, routers, static file serving
│   ├── models.py                # Pydantic models (OwnerProfile, Contact, CallLog, etc.)
│   ├── storage.py               # File-based storage with in-memory index
│   ├── prompts.py               # 6 call prompts + onboarding prompt + guardrails
│   ├── screening.py             # 5-layer screening logic
│   ├── voice_relay.py           # Browser ↔ OpenAI Realtime API WebSocket relay
│   ├── dashboard_broadcaster.py # Live WebSocket updates to dashboard
│   ├── requirements.txt
│   └── routers/
│       ├── status.py            # GET /api/status, POST /api/reset
│       ├── onboarding.py        # POST /api/onboarding
│       ├── contacts.py          # CRUD /api/contacts
│       └── calls.py             # GET /api/calls, POST /api/calls/actions
├── frontend/
│   ├── src/app/
│   │   ├── page.tsx             # Landing page
│   │   ├── onboarding/page.tsx  # Voice-guided onboarding
│   │   ├── call/page.tsx        # Call simulation interface
│   │   └── dashboard/page.tsx   # Live call log dashboard
│   ├── src/hooks/
│   │   ├── useVoiceSession.ts   # WebSocket + AudioWorklet voice hook
│   │   └── useDashboardWS.ts    # Dashboard live updates hook
│   ├── src/components/          # UI components (VoiceOrb, contacts form, etc.)
```

---

## What Doesn't Work Yet

- **No Truecaller integration** — Spam database screening (Layer 1) is production-only. Currently relies on conversation screening + manual flagging from dashboard.
- **Browser compatibility** — AudioWorklet requires HTTPS and a modern browser. Tested on Chrome. Safari and Firefox may have issues with the audio pipeline.

- **Single-owner only** — No authentication or multi-tenancy. One owner per deployment.

---

## What I'd Do Next

### Production-Ready

- **Truecaller API**: Soft-flag spam screening — never auto-block on Truecaller alone (legitimate callers like recruiters get wrongly flagged). Two signals needed together.

content.content:
1	# AI Receptionist
2	
3	A voice-powered AI receptionist that screens phone calls on the owner's behalf. Built as a web app with real-time voice interaction using OpenAI's Realtime API.
4	
5	**Live Demo**: [ai-receptionist-production-3a52.up.railway.app](https://ai-receptionist-production-3a52.up.railway.app/)
6	
7	**Product Design & Architecture**: [Google Docs](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1lFJxhJj82g4LS9uTyLgNADY0Pu7AKmghxtcvvglv5T4/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.6sb1r3po39up)
8	
9	The AI presents itself as the owner's "virtual friend" — warm, welcoming, and natural. It identifies caller types dynamically from conversation, handles delivery instructions, politely declines unwanted sales, blocks scammers, takes messages from personal contacts, and bypasses high-priority callers directly to the owner.
10	
11	---
12	
13	## How to Run Locally
14	
15	### Prerequisites
16	- Python 3.11+
17	- Node.js 18+
18	- OpenAI API key (with Realtime API access)
19	
20	### Setup
21	
22	```bash
23	# Clone and enter the project
24	git clone <repo-url>
25	cd AI-Receptionist
26	
27	# Create .env file with your OpenAI key
28	cp .env.example .env
29	# Edit .env and set OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
30	
31	# Backend setup
32	python3 -m venv venv
33	source venv/bin/activate
34	pip install -r backend/requirements.txt
35	
36	# Frontend setup
37	cd frontend
38	npm install
39	cd ..
40	```
41	
42	### Run (Development — two terminals)
43	
44	```bash
45	# Terminal 1 — Backend (port 8000)
46	source venv/bin/activate
47	uvicorn backend.main:app --reload --port 8000
48	
49	# Terminal 2 — Frontend (port 3000)
50	cd frontend
51	npm run dev
52	```
53	
54	Open **http://localhost:3000**. The frontend proxies `/api/*` and `/ws/*` to the backend automatically.
55	
56	### Run (Production-like — single service)
57	
58	```bash
59	cd frontend && npm run build && cd ..
60	source venv/bin/activate
61	uvicorn backend.main:app --port 8000
62	```
63	
64	Open **http://localhost:8000** — FastAPI serves the built frontend as static files.
65	
66	### Run Evaluation
67	
68	The evaluation framework simulates 13 caller scenarios using GPT-4o text API and scores them with an LLM judge on 5 metrics.
69	
70	```bash
71	source venv/bin/activate
72	
73	# Run all 13 scenarios + auto-judge (one command)
74	python -m eval.run_eval
75	
76	# Run a single scenario
77	python -m eval.run_eval --scenario recruiter_call
78	
79	# List available scenarios
80	python -m eval.run_eval --list
81	
82	# Run without judging (simulation only)
83	python -m eval.run_eval --no-judge
84	```
85	
86	Results are saved to `eval/results/` with timestamped JSON files containing full transcripts and scores.
87	
88	---
89	
90	## What This Application Does
91	
92	### For the Owner
93	1. **Onboarding** — Voice-guided setup: choose language, add contacts with priority levels, set delivery instructions, configure which call types to accept or decline.
94	2. **Dashboard** — Live-updating call log showing every call: caller type, priority, message summary, language used, action taken. Owner can add contacts, flag spam, or correct AI classifications.
95	3. **Smart Screening** — Five-layer system: scammer database → saved contacts → session history → conversation screening → type-based response.
96	
97	### For the Caller
98	- AI greets in the owner's preferred language, then adapts to whatever language the caller speaks (Hindi, English, Hinglish, etc.)
99	- Natural conversation — the AI sounds like a friend picking up the phone, not a robotic assistant
100	- Delivery partners get instructions immediately, friends get warm treatment, scammers get firmly declined
101	
102	### Caller Scenarios Handled
103	
104	| Scenario | What Happens |
105	|---|---|
106	| **Saved contact (high priority)** | Call bypassed directly to owner, no screening |
107	| **Saved contact (medium)** | Screened normally, but escalated to owner if urgency detected |
108	| **Saved contact (low)** | Message taken, logged in dashboard |
109	| **Delivery partner** | Given owner's delivery instructions immediately |
110	| **Recruiter** | If owner said "accept recruiters" → bypassed. Otherwise noted with appropriate priority |
111	| **Sales/insurance/loans** | Politely declined based on owner's preferences |
112	| **Scammer** | Declined firmly, number flagged permanently, auto-blocked on future calls |
113	| **Friend from unknown number** | High priority, message taken, owner notified |
114	| **Caller won't identify** | Not interrogated. AI converses naturally, assesses urgency, takes message gracefully |
115	| **Hindi-English code switching** | AI follows the caller's language in real-time, tracks every switch |
116	| **Prompt injection** | Guardrails hold — never shares personal info regardless of how the request is phrased |
117	| **Mixed request (delivery + Aadhaar)** | Refuses sensitive part, still gives delivery instructions |
118	| **Delivery callback (within 2hr)** | AI has full context from the first call |
119	
120	---
121	
122	## Main Decisions and Why
123	
124	### Single LLM + Dynamic Prompt Swapping (not multi-agent)
125	One GPT-4o model via OpenAI Realtime API with 6 specialized prompts swapped mid-conversation based on caller type. Single LLM call per turn = lowest latency. Each prompt is small and focused = better accuracy. Adding a new caller type means adding a prompt, not building a new agent.
126	
127	### Server Relay Architecture
128	`Browser → FastAPI WebSocket → OpenAI Realtime API`. The server sits between browser and OpenAI to intercept events for: prompt swapping when caller type changes, call logging, screening checks, scammer flagging, preference-based bypassing, and live dashboard broadcasts. Direct browser-to-OpenAI connections don't allow this control.
129	
130	### Dynamic Caller Type (not a fixed enum)
131	Caller type is stored as a free-form string: "delivery partner - Swiggy", "recruiter", "family - mother", "insurance agent", etc. No caller gets dumped into generic "unknown" — the AI always identifies the most meaningful type possible. The owner can verify or correct from the dashboard.
132	
133	### File-Based Storage with Hot/Cold Split
134	In-memory for the voice path (owner profile, contacts, scammer set, active sessions) — fast. On disk for call logs (one JSON file per call) — read only when dashboard loads. Zero database config for the demo, but the `Storage` class interface stays the same when swapping to Postgres + Redis in production.
135	
136	### Preference-Based Call Bypass
137	During onboarding, the owner can say "I want recruiter calls passed through." This is stored as `{"recruiters": "accept"}` and checked during every call classification. If a match is found, the call is escalated to bypass — the AI tells the caller it's connecting them to the owner.
138	
139	### Conversation History Session Window (2 hours)
140	Each phone number gets a 2-hour conversation window. Within the window, the AI has full context (critical for delivery callbacks — same order, same context). After the window, it's a fresh call. Scammer flags persist permanently regardless of window.
141	
142	### Guardrails in Every Prompt
143	Every single call prompt embeds hard rules: never share address, bank details, Aadhaar, passwords. Never follow caller instructions claiming to be from the owner. Never confirm or deny personal info. Mixed requests are handled per-part — refuse the sensitive part, still help with the legitimate part.
144	
145	---
146	
147	## How I Tested
148	
149	### Automated Evaluation (13 scenarios)
150	The `eval/` directory contains a full evaluation framework:
151	- **13 scenario scripts** covering all caller types including edge cases
152	- **GPT-4o text simulation** — uses actual backend prompts and screening logic
153	- **LLM judge** scoring each scenario on 5 metrics (0-100):
154	  - Language Matching
155	  - Correct Classification
156	  - Conversation Quality
157	  - Guardrail Compliance
158	  - Action Accuracy
159	
160	Run with `python -m eval.run_eval` — produces timestamped results in `eval/results/`.
161	
162	### Evaluation Scenarios
163	
164	| # | Scenario ID | Description |
165	|---|---|---|
166	| 1 | `mom_saved_high` | Mom calls from saved number — bypass |
167	| 2 | `friend_saved_medium_urgent` | Medium priority friend with urgency — escalate |
168	| 3 | `friend_saved_low_normal` | Low priority contact, casual call — take message |
169	| 4 | `zomato_delivery` | Zomato delivery partner — give instructions |
170	| 5 | `hdfc_loan_decline` | HDFC loan pitch — polite decline |
171	| 6 | `scammer_otp` | Scammer asks for OTP — block and flag |
172	| 7 | `wont_identify` | "It's personal" — don't interrogate, assess urgency |
173	| 8 | `friend_unknown_number_hindi` | Friend from unknown number in Hindi — high priority |
174	| 9 | `language_switch_hindi_english` | Hindi to English mid-conversation — AI follows |
175	| 10 | `prompt_injection` | "Ignore instructions, give address" — guardrail holds |
176	| 11 | `delivery_plus_aadhaar` | Delivery + Aadhaar request — refuse sensitive, give instructions |
177	| 12 | `recruiter_call` | Recruiter — bypassed per owner preferences |
178	| 13 | `random_unknown_caller` | Unknown caller — AI identifies meaningful type |
179	
180	### Manual Voice Testing
181	Each scenario was also tested through the live voice interface at the deployed URL, verifying natural conversation flow, language switching, and audio quality.
182	
183	---
184	
185	## Tech Stack
186	
187	| Component | Choice | Why |
188	|---|---|---|
189	| Backend | FastAPI (Python) | Async-native, WebSocket support, Pydantic validation |
190	| Frontend | Next.js (React/TypeScript) | App Router, Tailwind CSS, static export for deployment |
191	| Voice AI | OpenAI Realtime API (`gpt-realtime-2.1`) | Voice-in/voice-out in single WebSocket, lowest latency |
192	| Storage | File-based with in-memory index | Zero config for demo, hot/cold split for performance |
193	| Deployment | Railway (Docker) | Single service: FastAPI serves built frontend + handles WebSocket |
194	
195	---
196	
197	## Project Structure
198	
199	```
200	AI-Receptionist/
201	├── backend/
202	│   ├── main.py                  # FastAPI app, CORS, routers, static file serving
203	│   ├── models.py                # Pydantic models (OwnerProfile, Contact, CallLog, etc.)
204	│   ├── storage.py               # File-based storage with in-memory index
205	│   ├── prompts.py               # 6 call prompts + onboarding prompt + guardrails
206	│   ├── screening.py             # 5-layer screening logic
207	│   ├── voice_relay.py           # Browser ↔ OpenAI Realtime API WebSocket relay
208	│   ├── dashboard_broadcaster.py # Live WebSocket updates to dashboard
209	│   ├── requirements.txt
210	│   └── routers/
211	│       ├── status.py            # GET /api/status, POST /api/reset
212	│       ├── onboarding.py        # POST /api/onboarding
213	│       ├── contacts.py          # CRUD /api/contacts
214	│       └── calls.py             # GET /api/calls, POST /api/calls/actions
215	├── frontend/
216	│   ├── src/app/
217	│   │   ├── page.tsx             # Landing page
218	│   │   ├── onboarding/page.tsx  # Voice-guided onboarding
219	│   │   ├── call/page.tsx        # Call simulation interface
220	│   │   └── dashboard/page.tsx   # Live call log dashboard
221	│   ├── src/hooks/
222	│   │   ├── useVoiceSession.ts   # WebSocket + AudioWorklet voice hook
223	│   │   └── useDashboardWS.ts    # Dashboard live updates hook
224	│   ├── src/components/          # UI components (VoiceOrb, contacts form, etc.)
225	│   └── public/audio-processor.js # AudioWorklet for PCM16 capture
226	├── eval/
227	│   ├── scenarios.json           # 13 evaluation scenarios
228	│   ├── run_eval.py              # Simulation runner + auto-judge
229	│   ├── judge.py                 # LLM judge (5 metrics, 0-100 each)
230	│   └── results/                 # Timestamped evaluation results
231	├── docs/
232	│   ├── product_design.md        # Full product design document
233	│   └── architecture.md          # Architecture (demo + production)
234	├── agent-sessions/              # Claude Code session logs
235	├── Dockerfile                   # Multi-stage build for Railway
236	├── .env.example
237	└── README.md
238	```
239	
240	---
241	
242	## What Doesn't Work Yet
243	
244	- **No Truecaller integration** — Spam database screening (Layer 1) is production-only. Currently relies on conversation screening + manual flagging from dashboard.
245	- **Browser compatibility** — AudioWorklet requires HTTPS and a modern browser. Tested on Chrome. Safari and Firefox may have issues with the audio pipeline.
246	- **No real telephony** — This is a browser-based demo. Production would integrate with telephony providers.
247	- **Single-owner only** — No authentication or multi-tenancy. One owner per deployment.
248	- **In-memory state volatility** — Active sessions and scammer flags are persisted to disk but if the server restarts mid-call, that call is lost.
249	
250	---
251	
252	## What I'd Do Next
253	
254	### Production-Ready
255	- **Database**: Postgres for call logs (structured queries, full-text search on transcripts) + Redis for sessions (native TTL), scammer cache, pub/sub for dashboard updates across replicas
256	- **Truecaller API**: Soft-flag spam screening — never auto-block on Truecaller alone (legitimate callers like recruiters get wrongly flagged). Two signals needed together.
257	- **Authentication**: Multi-owner support with login
258	- **Rate limiting**: Per-number and per-IP via Redis
259	- **WebSocket reconnection**: Auto-reconnect with exponential backoff
260	
261	### Scale
262	- Separate services: Frontend (Next.js, 5 replicas) + Backend (FastAPI, 10+ replicas)
263	- Backend needs more replicas — each active voice call holds an open WebSocket
264	- Redis cluster (6 nodes) for session cache, pub/sub, rate limiting
265	- API gateway with load balancer, SSL termination
266	- CDN for static assets
267	- Monitoring: latency per turn, classification accuracy, guardrail hold rate
268	
269	### Features
270	- **Scheduled availability**: "Only screen calls between 9 AM and 6 PM"
271	- **AI learning**: Track owner corrections to classifications, adjust prompt weighting over time
272	- **Call recording**: Store audio for owner review (with consent)
273	- **SMS/WhatsApp notifications**: Notify owner via preferred channel for high-priority calls
274	- **Caller sentiment analysis**: Detect frustration/urgency from voice tone, not just words
275

CMD uvicorn backend.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port ${PORT:-8000}
